zuspecial

Overview

R’s special functions are scattered. Base R has the gamma function and Bessel functions of real argument; complex Bessel functions, hypergeometric functions, elliptic integrals and the Lambert W function each live in their own package, or in gsl, which needs the GNU Scientific Library installed. And when a model is written in Python and checked in R, or the other way round, two libraries that disagree in the last digits are a needless source of doubt.

zuspecial gives R the special functions of scipy.special, computed by the same C++ kernels: xsf, the library SciPy’s special functions are built from, at the commit SciPy 1.18.1 uses.

  • SciPy’s values. Each function is tested against xsref’s mpmath reference tables, under xsf’s own tolerances, and against SciPy 1.18.1 itself, on Linux, macOS and Windows.
  • Real and complex arguments. Bessel, Hankel, Airy, gamma, error, exponential-integral, hypergeometric and zeta functions take complex arguments where SciPy does.
  • SciPy’s names and argument order. sc_jv(v, z) is scipy.special.jv(v, z), so code translates line by line.
  • Ordinary R functions. Vectorised and recycled, NA-aware, keeping names and dimensions; floating-point conditions follow SciPy’s seterr(), as warnings or errors when asked for.
  • A C interface. Other packages can call the functions from compiled code through LinkingTo: zuspecial.

Nothing is needed at run time; Boost.Math headers, from the BH package, are needed to build it.

Installation

zuspecial is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub with:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zuspecial")

Usage 

library(zuspecial)

Functions are vectorised, and take complex arguments where SciPy does:

sc_gamma(c(0.5, 5))
#> [1]  1.772454 24.000000
sc_gamma(1 + 1i)
#> [1] 0.4980157-0.1549498i

Arguments come in SciPy’s order, the order first for the Bessel functions, where base R’s besselJ() puts it second:

sc_jv(2.5, 3)
#> [1] 0.41271
besselJ(3, 2.5)
#> [1] 0.41271

As in SciPy, the type of the argument picks the result: the Bessel function of order 0.5 at -1 is NaN for a real -1, and a complex number for -1+0i:

sc_jv(0.5, -1)
#> [1] NaN
sc_jv(0.5, -1 + 0i)
#> [1] 5.551115e-17+0.6713967i

Poles, overflow and loss of precision are silent by default, as in SciPy, and can be turned into warnings or errors:

sc_gamma(-1)
#> [1] NaN
sc_errstate(sc_gamma(-1), singular = "warn")
#> Warning in sc_gamma(-1): sc_gamma: singular in 1 element, first at index 1.
#> [1] NaN

Functions that return several values in SciPy return a named list:

str(sc_airy(1))
#> List of 4
#>  $ ai : num 0.135
#>  $ aip: num -0.159
#>  $ bi : num 1.21
#>  $ bip: num 0.932

Every function is sc_ followed by its name in scipy.special, the alias SciPy’s own documentation uses (import scipy.special as sc).

Acknowledgements

The kernels are SciPy’s xsf, with its bundled Cephes, AMOS, specfun, Faddeeva and qd code, and Boost.Math for the functions SciPy evaluates with it. The reference values come from xsref. zuspecial is also checked against the gsl, Bessel, hypergeo, lamW, expint and Rmpfr packages.
